Britain's King Charles III delivers a speech during the 28th Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) opening ceremony at the National Performing Arts Centre, in St John's, Antigua and Barbuda, on November 3, 2026 [Ben Stansall/AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff and APPublished On 3 Nov 20263 Nov 2026
King Charles III has said at the official opening of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda that the transatlantic slave trade fills him with “horror” and “the most profound personal sorrow”.
The British monarch said on Tuesday that the slave trade “still casts a shadow over these [Caribbean] islands and other members of our Commonwealth”, and that the Royal Navy had played “a leading role” in ending it.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Does the UK have a legal obligation to redress the harms of slavery?list 2 of 3King Charles’s Caribbean tour: Will he discuss slavery reparations?list 3 of 3King Charles on Caribbean tour as calls grow for slavery reparationsend of list
“We cannot change the actions of those who came before us,” Charles said. “We can, however, learn from the past.”
The king said he was seeking ways to address the wrongs by improving access to education, investing in jobs, encouraging trade among Commonwealth countries and pushing for climate resilience.
He ended the speech short of the apology that many Caribbean and African countries had hoped for. He offered no measures to address the economic and social damage of slavery.
Buckingham Palace had said the king would not issue a formal apology for slavery during his Caribbean tour, which also took him to the Bahamas and Guyana.
Guyanese President Mohamed Irfaan Ali said in an interview that an apology should be the king’s next step.

Trump plans for ‘massive’ resource exploration in GreenlandBy Al Jazeera Staff and APPublished On 3 Nov 20263 Nov 2026
Lawmakers in the semi-autonomous Danish territory of Greenland have approved an agreement with Denmark and the United States aimed at bolstering security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
The deal was passed 16-0 on Tuesday, with seven lawmakers abstaining.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3US signs ‘tremendous’ security deal with Denmark and Greenlandlist 2 of 3Why does Greenland matter to the US?list 3 of 3Greenland’s delegation gets hero’s welcome after signing US-Denmark pactend of list
The agreement was signed in September by US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
It followed months of negotiations behind the scenes amid growing tensions over Trump’s repeated threats to seize the vast, resource-rich Arctic island.
Greenlandic Foreign Minister Mute Egede said the ratification was another important step for the self-governing island.
“The road to this point has been ⁠a difficult one for us as ⁠a people. But we have stood firm on our fundamental principles, chosen dialogue and taken responsibility for our country’s interests,” he wrote in a ⁠post on Facebook.
“This is about all of us. The Greenland we love. ⁠About our security. And about our ⁠right to shape our own future,” he said.An aerial view of houses and apartment buildings in Nuuk, Greenland [File: Sean Gallup/Getty Images]
Located between Europe and North America, Greenland is the world’s largest island, with a population of 57,000 people.

Shrimp boats docked at Shem Creek, in Mount Pleasant, South Carolina [Catherine Nouhan/Al Jazeera]By Catherine NouhanPublished On 3 Nov 20263 Nov 2026
Mount Pleasant, South Carolina – For Mark Marhefka, the weather can be the difference between a profitable fishing trip and a dangerous one.
As a shrimper and fisherman for 49 years, Marhefka relies on forecasts, weather buoys and data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to decide when it is safe to take his boats offshore. With storms and warm water temperatures disrupting this year’s fishing season, he worries that President Donald Trump’s proposed funding cuts could further reduce the services fishermen depend on.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3China to suspend imports of Japanese seafood amid diplomatic row: Reportslist 2 of 3Trump administration aims to cut regulations on US commercial fishinglist 3 of 3Lobster industry caught in Maine’s political headwinds before US midtermsend of list
“They’ve already started cutting back on NOAA, and they’re looking to do more in this next fiscal year,” Marhefka, who owns Abundant Seafood, told Al Jazeera. “It’s definitely something that we need to fight against.”
Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, NOAA has lost roughly 20 percent of its workforce, according to an analysis of federal employment data. The administration’s proposed 2027 budget would cut funding for ocean monitoring and terminate a programme supporting regional ocean observations.
But the weather is only one of the pressures facing South Carolina shrimpers as they head to the polls on Tuesday for the US midterm elections.

Displaced people ride a an animal-drawn cart, following Rapid Support Forces (RSF) attacks on Zamzam displacement camp, in the town of Tawila, North Darfur, Sudan April 15, 2025 [File: Stringer/Reuters]By Mohamed Zakaria KhamisPublished On 3 Nov 20263 Nov 2026
In a small house in Omdurman, Hassan Saber Jumaa, a senior administrator at the Zamzam displacement camp in Sudan, sat on a simple wooden chair. He scrolled through his phone, looking for any photograph he might have of Zamzam, which is near el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, and once sheltered hundreds of thousands.
He found nothing. Jumaa explained that his old phone was looted during last year’s attack by Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces on the camp. Pointing to the bare walls around him, Jumaa said that all he has left are his memories of the camp, and the people who once called it home.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Deadly RSF drone attacks reveal deep divisions between Sudan and Ethiopialist 2 of 3Sudan’s displaced return to new challenges in war-battered Khartoumlist 3 of 3Drone attacks extend campaign targeting Sudan’s power systemend of list
Zamzam, established in 2004, was home to generations of people displaced by western Sudan’s Darfur war, which began in 2003 and continued for nearly two decades. Alongside Abu Shouk camp and al-Salam camp, Zamzam formed part of one of Darfur’s largest concentrations of displaced people.
Jumaa recalled a bustling community, with its market open every day, and children walking to school.
Zamzam memories

Protesters hold portraits of Benjamin Netanyahu during a demonstration in support of the Israeli prime minister at Habima Square in Tel Aviv on October 31, 2026, following Israel's general election [Jack Guez/AFP]By Simon Speakman CordallPublished On 3 Nov 20263 Nov 2026
Israel’s election results are due to be certified on Wednesday, but with both leading blocs falling short of a parliamentary majority, negotiations remain deadlocked.
As things stand, the right-wing coalition of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured 53 seats in the October 27 vote, while the self-styled Zionist opposition alliance led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot had 48. A majority requires 61 seats in the 120-strong Knesset. The 19 remaining seats went to the two Arab-led lists – the Joint List and Ra’am, or the United Arab List.

Netanyahu’s camp has been accused of seeking to delegitimise the results after launching a series of largely discounted claims that the vote for the Arab parties, which scored their best-ever electoral performance, had been manipulated by foreign interference.
Despite their historic showing that was boosted by an unprecedented surge in voter turnout, the two Arab-led lists remain politically isolated.
